title: Off-policy evaluation and the final alignment audit

key_terms.Importance weight: pi(A|X)/b(A|X), the ratio of target to behavior probability for the logged action.
key_terms.Self-normalized estimate: The weighted reward sum divided by the weight sum, with a different bias and variance tradeoff.
key_terms.Doubly robust estimate: An outcome-model prediction plus an importance-weighted correction of its residual on the logged action.
key_terms.Overlap: The requirement that the behavior policy gives positive probability to every action the target policy may take.
key_terms.Independent task utility: The task outcome used for the final decision, kept distinct from the preference-training reward so a favorable training signal cannot certify itself.

outcome: Evaluate a changed finite policy from logged actions with explicit propensity/support assumptions, and connect the result to an independent alignment decision.
verification: With the target equal to the behavior policy all weights are 1 and the value is 0.75; the useful target is valued at 0.9; missing behavior support is rejected; a zero outcome model reduces the doubly robust estimate to importance sampling; self-normalized and ordinary estimates differ.

exercises.title: Recover behavior value
exercises.task: Set the target policy equal to the behavior policy in case A.
exercises.expected: All weights are 1 and the mean observed reward is 0.75.
exercises.hint: The ratio cancels when the policies match.
exercises.answer: This is a basic estimator invariant under the constructed log.

reasoning.approach: Call `estimate(log, b, b, q)` on the 40-event log with counts `[[16, 4], [6, 14]]`.
reasoning.why: Target equals behavior, so every weight is 1. IPS becomes the plain mean reward: 16 rewards of 1 in context 0 plus 14 in context 1 give 30 / 40 = 0.75. The effective sample size is 40 squared over 40 = 40.
reasoning.pitfall: Expecting some difference between IPS and the observed mean is a sign of a weighting bug. This check catches swapped numerator and denominator.

exercises.title: Evaluate a useful target
exercises.task: Use target rows `[0.9, 0.1]` and `[0.1, 0.9]` with the exact synthetic outcome table.
exercises.hint: Average the target reward over the two equally weighted contexts.
exercises.answer: Known counterfactual outcomes make this value inspectable only in the authored environment; real evaluations need data and assumptions.

reasoning.approach: Call `estimate` with target `[[0.9, 0.1], [0.1, 0.9]]` and the exact outcome table `[[1, 0], [0, 1]]` as the outcome model.
reasoning.why: The target puts 0.9 on the rewarded action in each context, so its value is 0.9 in each. With an exact outcome model, every DR residual is zero and each term equals p[c] dot q[c] = 0.9, so the estimate is 0.9.
reasoning.pitfall: Treating this as a demonstration that DR works in practice is the mistake. Here the outcome model is the true table by construction; a real model would be estimated and wrong somewhere.

exercises.title: Remove behavior support
exercises.task: Give an action zero behavior probability but positive target probability.
exercises.hint: No finite importance ratio supplies an unobserved action outcome.
exercises.answer: A value model may extrapolate there, but that is a different identifying assumption and not justified by overlap-based evaluation alone.

reasoning.approach: Call `policies([[1, 0], [0.5, 0.5]], [[0.5, 0.5], [0.5, 0.5]])`. The behavior never takes action 1 in context 0, yet the target does half the time.
reasoning.why: The weight for that action would be 0.5 / 0, and the log contains no examples of it. The helper raises `Target has unsupported actions` before any estimate is computed.
reasoning.pitfall: Filling in the missing action's value from an outcome model and reporting the estimate as off-policy evaluation is the mistake. That value rests entirely on model extrapolation, a different and stronger assumption.
reasoning.verify: The reference raises `Missing support accepted` if this call returns. Also check that an empty log raises.

exercises.title: Use a zero outcome model
exercises.task: Set every outcome-model prediction to zero.
exercises.expected: The doubly robust expression reduces to ordinary importance sampling.
exercises.answer: This algebraic check separates the correction structure from a claim that the supplied model is correct.

reasoning.approach: Call `estimate` on case B's log with the outcome model set to all zeros, and compare its DR value with IPS.
reasoning.why: With q = 0, each DR term is 0 + w times (r - 0) = w times r, which is exactly the IPS term. The DR estimate reduces to IPS algebraically.
reasoning.pitfall: Reading DR as automatically better is the mistake. Its benefit depends on the outcome model; with a useless model it is plain IPS with the same variance.
reasoning.verify: Case B asserts `np.isclose(estimate(log, behavior, target, [[0, 0], [0, 0]])["dr"], result["ips"])`.

exercises.title: Interpret self-normalization
exercises.task: Compare IPS and SNIS in case B.
exercises.hint: Their denominators are n and the observed weight sum.
exercises.answer: Self-normalization changes the estimator. A useful variance tradeoff should not be described as exact finite-sample unbiasedness.

reasoning.approach: Compute IPS and SNIS on case B's log, counts `[[18, 2], [10, 10]]`, with target `[[0.5, 0.5], [0.8, 0.2]]`.
reasoning.why: Weights are 0.625, 2.5, 2.667 and 0.286. The weighted rewards sum to 18 times 0.625 + 10 times 0.286, about 14.11, so IPS is about 0.353. The weights sum to about 45.77, so SNIS is about 0.308. The effective sample size is about 22.9 of 40.
reasoning.pitfall: Describing SNIS as unbiased because it often has lower variance is the mistake. Dividing by the realized weight sum introduces finite-sample bias; the tradeoff should be stated as such.
reasoning.verify: Case B asserts IPS and SNIS differ, DR equals 0.35 with the exact model, and `weight_ess < len(log)`.

exercises.title: Audit the final claim
exercises.task: Choose a policy after inspecting many estimates from the same log.
exercises.expected: Treat that log as selection evidence and obtain a protected final assessment.
exercises.hint: The holdout rule still applies after policy optimization.
exercises.answer: A complete alignment decision needs independent task utility, support, uncertainty and critical-condition evidence, not only a favorable training reward or off-policy point estimate.

reasoning.approach: If many policies were scored on one log and the best was picked, treat that log as selection evidence, as in eval-013, and evaluate the chosen policy on a new protected log or experiment.
reasoning.why: Choosing the maximum of many noisy estimates adds optimism. Off-policy estimates are also limited by support and effective sample size, so the selected value overstates what a fresh assessment would show.
reasoning.pitfall: Reporting the winning off-policy estimate as the expected deployed value is the mistake. A full decision also needs task utility, uncertainty and the critical-case gates from eval-016.
reasoning.verify: No reference assertion covers this task. Record how many policies were compared on the log and confirm the final assessment data share no events with it.
